extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students of mathematical analysis and differential geometry (surfaces)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and technical criteria for ruled surfaces, envelopes of families of surfaces, maxima/minima of functions of two variables, and curvature of curves traced on a surface; contains definitions, necessary-and-sufficient conditions, and worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for developable (développable) ruled surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition (i): da·dk - db·dh = 0 for a generator (expressed in text as "da dk — db dh = 0"); when this condition is satisfied for a given generator the tangent plane is the same at every point along that generator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this condition holds for all generators (for all values of the parameter u) the ruled surface is called 'développable'; the generators then have an envelope called the arête de rebroussement. If the condition fails for (generic) generators the surface is 'gauche' (skew) and the generators have no envelope. Example: a parametrized straight line giving a = -p, b = -p, h = u, k = -u yields da·dk - db·dh = 0 identically (developable). Conversely, an example producing a nonzero expression (thus gauche) is provided in the text. The exceptional case where m is independent of z is exactly this condition; then the tangent plane is identical at all points of the generator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature sign for developable vs skew ruled surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Developable surfaces have zero total curvature at every point (k1·k2 = 0), while skew (gauche) ruled surfaces have negative total curvature at each point (k1·k2 < 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric reason: on a developable surface the tangent plane along a generator cuts the surface in two coincident lines (generator of contact) as in cones and cylinders, giving total curvature zero; on a gauche surface the tangent plane varies along a generator producing negative total curvature (examples: hyperboloid of one or two sheets mentioned).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition for interior extremum of f(x,y): vanishing first partials
rubrics_metrics.description: For f(x,y) to have a maximum or minimum at (a,b) it is necessary that the first partial derivatives vanish at that point: p = f_x(a,b) = 0 and q = f_y(a,b) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is derived by Taylor-expanding f(a+x', b+y') and noting that if linear terms in x',y' were present they would change sign under small displacements; hence p and q must be zero (equivalently, the tangent plane is horizontal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-derivative (discriminant) test for extrema of function of two variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Let r,f''_{xx}=r, s=f''_{xy}=s, t=f''_{yy}=t at (a,b). Define discriminant Δ = r·t - s^2 (text uses notation rt - s^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If p = q = 0 and Δ > 0 then (a,b) is an extremum: if r < 0 (or t < 0) it's a maximum; if r > 0 (or t > 0) it's a minimum. If Δ < 0 the point is a saddle (neither max nor min). If Δ = 0 the case is doubtful: higher-order terms must be examined (examples in text show both neither-extremum and minimum occurring when Δ = 0 depending on higher terms). Geometric interpretation: Δ > 0 means the surface has positive total curvature at the point (lies on one side of the tangent plane); the sign of r (or t) determines whether it's below/above giving max/min.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic method for testing extrema via Taylor expansion and polar substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Taylor expansion of f about (a,b) up to second order, then set x' = ρ cosφ, y' = ρ sinφ and examine the sign of the quadratic form in cosφ, sinφ multiplied by ρ^2 for small ρ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method shows why first-order coefficients must vanish and reduces the test to sign of the quadratic form (Δ and r/t signs). If the quadratic form is identically a perfect square (Δ = 0) one must inspect higher-order terms in ρ; the text provides worked examples showing how to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Envelope of a one-parameter family of surfaces — characteristic equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given F(x,y,z,λ) = 0 describing a family S_λ, the characteristic curves (where each S_λ touches the envelope E) are defined by the simultaneous equations F = 0 and ∂F/∂λ = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The envelope E is the locus of these characteristic curves; eliminating the parameter λ between F = 0 and F_λ = 0 yields the equation of the envelope (or possibly the locus of singular points). The characteristic is the limit of the intersection curve of S_λ with a nearby surface S_{λ+dλ} as dλ → 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arête de rebroussement (edge of regression) for one-parameter families
rubrics_metrics.description: When the family of surfaces has characteristics whose envelope exists, that envelope (as λ varies) is the arête de rebroussement A of the envelope surface; the points of A are determined by solving F = 0, F_λ = 0, and F_{λλ} = 0 (or equivalently the reduction to the three equations (A) in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: form F = 0, F_λ = 0, and the derivative of F_λ (i.e. second derivative with respect to λ) and solve for x,y,z as functions of λ; as λ varies the solution traces the edge. If the solutions are imaginary for all λ, the edge does not exist (is imaginary). Example: for a moving plane A(λ)x + B(λ)y + C(λ)z + D(λ)=0 the characteristic is a straight line given by the plane equation and its derivative; the envelope is a developable surface and the arête is given by the three relations including second derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developable surfaces as envelopes of a one-parameter family of planes
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-parameter moving plane envelopes a developable surface; the moving plane is the osculating plane to the arête de rebroussement, and conversely any developable surface is the envelope of its tangent planes (the osculating planes to its edge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the plane equation and its derivatives with respect to the parameter one obtains equations determining the edge of regression. The characteristics (generatrices) of the developable are straight lines (intersections of adjacent planes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Envelope (canal surface) of spheres with fixed radius centered on a curve
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centers of spheres of fixed radius R describe a curve C (center coordinates a(u), b(u), c(u)), then the envelope of those spheres is a canal surface; the characteristic on each sphere is the circle obtained by intersecting the sphere with the normal plane at the center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric description: the envelope is obtained by taking on each normal to the curve C lengths equal to R (both directions), producing the parallel surface to C. The arête de rebroussement of the canal surface may be imaginary if R is sufficiently small. The characteristic is determined by F=0 and derivative with respect to parameter (see text equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Envelope of a two-parameter family of surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: For F(x,y,z;λ,μ)=0 (two parameters), a surface envelope (if it exists) is obtained by solving the three simultaneous equations F = 0, ∂F/∂λ = 0, ∂F/∂μ = 0 and eliminating λ and μ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elimination may yield an actual envelope or the locus of singular points of the mobile surfaces; examples in the text (plane depending on two parameters) yield explicit envelopes (e.g., a paraboloid). For spheres of fixed radius whose centers run over a surface, the envelope (surface parallèle) is obtained similarly by equating normals and distances (text gives the geometric interpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem I — curvature equivalence with plane section by osculating plane
rubrics_metrics.description: At a point A on a surface, the radius of curvature R_φ of any curve through A on the surface equals the radius of curvature of the plane section obtained by intersecting the surface with the osculating plane of that curve at A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: to find the curvature of any surface curve at A one may compute the curvature of the corresponding planar section by the osculating plane. The text derives the formula for the curvature using Frenet formulas and partial derivatives of z(x,y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meusnier's theorem (Theorem II) for oblique sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The center of curvature G_φ of an oblique (non-normal) section of a surface is the orthogonal projection onto the plane of that oblique section of the center of curvature C of the corresponding normal section. Quantitatively R_φ = R·cosθ (or R_φ = R·cos(π-θ) when cosθ negative), where θ is the angle between the plane of the oblique section and the normal section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation and proof: choose coordinates so AN is the surface normal and measure θ as the dihedral angle between the plane of the oblique section and the normal section; the relation R_φ = R cosθ shows how curvatures of oblique sections relate to normal-section curvature. The theorem is illustrated and sign cases (acute/obtuse θ) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign convention and formula for radii of curvature of normal sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt sign convention: radius R of a normal section is positive when the center of curvature lies on the chosen positive half of the normal AN, negative otherwise. With this convention a single formula gives R (text presents formula (7): R = [sqrt(1 + p^2 + q^2)] / (a^2 + ... denominator expression) — full formula in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: if rt - s^2 > 0 (total curvature positive at A) then the denominator of R keeps a constant sign and all normal sections have centers on the same side of A. If rt - s^2 < 0 (total curvature negative) the denominator changes sign with direction and there exist two special normal sections (asymptotic directions) for which R is infinite (centers at infinity) — these are the directions AD and AD' (asymptotic tangents).
